explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Moses says, “The fruit of your womb will be cursed, as well as the produce of your land, the calves of your herds, and the lambs of your flocks.” (Deuteronomy 28:18). Family, fields and flocks are all named in that verse. Just before it, he says they will be cursed in the city and cursed in the country (Deuteronomy 28:16).

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “The fruit of your womb will be cursed, as well as the produce of your land, the calves of your herds, and the lambs of your flocks.” (Deuteronomy 28:18). He names the children, the crops and the animals. I think it's a heavy list, and it starts with the children.

explanations.answer: Everything they put their hand to
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD will send “…confusion and reproof in all to which you put your hand…” (Deuteronomy 28:20). Moses doesn't narrow that to one kind of work. He says it lasts until they are destroyed and quickly perish because of the wickedness they have committed in forsaking Him.

explanations.answer: Their fields but not their homes
explanations.explanation: Close, but Moses doesn't draw that line. He says confusion and reproof come “…in all to which you put your hand…” (Deuteronomy 28:20). Homes aren't left out of that. Even the basket and kneading bowl were named earlier (Deuteronomy 28:17).

explanations.answer: Their homes but not their fields
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't split it that way, friend. He says confusion and reproof come “…in all to which you put your hand…” (Deuteronomy 28:20). That takes in the fields too. The produce of their land is named as cursed in Deuteronomy 28:18.

That's the one, baker. Moses says the curses come because of “…the wickedness you have committed in forsaking Him.” (Deuteronomy 28:20). Forsaking means walking away from the LORD. Moses names that as the reason.
Not quite, friend. Moses says “…the wickedness you have committed in forsaking Him.” (Deuteronomy 28:20). The word is forsaking, which means walking away. Fearing isn't what the verse says.

Good try, but the verse says something else. Moses speaks of “…the wickedness you have committed in forsaking Him.” (Deuteronomy 28:20). Forsaking is leaving the LORD behind. Thanking never shows up in that line.

Yes, baker. Moses says the LORD will turn the rain of their land “…into dust and powder…” (Deuteronomy 28:24). I know a little about dust, since I sat under years of it in a junk drawer. Rain that comes down as powder is no kind of rain.
Not this time, friend. Moses says the rain becomes dust and powder, and it descends from the sky until they are destroyed (Deuteronomy 28:24). He doesn't mention hail or ice. It's dry, dry, dry.

I see why that sounds fitting with a bronze sky. But Moses says the LORD will turn the rain into dust and powder (Deuteronomy 28:24). No fire or smoke is named in that verse. Just dry, dusty stuff coming down.

I'd flip that one, baker. Moses says the LORD will cause Israel to be defeated before their enemies. They will march out against them in one direction but flee from them in seven (Deuteronomy 28:25). Israel is the one running, and in seven directions at that.

Yes, baker. It's Israel who does the fleeing. Moses says, “You will march out against them in one direction but flee from them in seven.” (Deuteronomy 28:25). They go out one way and run seven ways. In that verse, the LORD is the one who causes them to be defeated before their enemies.
Yes, baker. Moses says, “You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.” (Deuteronomy 28:25). That's what defeat looks like to everyone watching. It's a heavy line.

That's the opposite picture, friend. Moses says they will be defeated, and then, “You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.” (Deuteronomy 28:25). The word he uses is horror. Being a nation to be feared isn't what the verse says.
I can see how you got there. But Moses says, “You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.” (Deuteronomy 28:25). The word is horror. Pity isn't in the verse.
Moses says the opposite, baker. Day after day they will be oppressed and plundered, “…with no one to save you.” (Deuteronomy 28:29). No rescuer shows up in that verse. It's a hard one.

Right, baker. Moses says they will be oppressed and plundered day after day, “…with no one to save you.” (Deuteronomy 28:29). Nobody comes to the rescue in that picture. It's a heavy moment, and I'll leave it at that.

explanations.answer: He will not live in it
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says, “You will build a house but will not live in it.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). All that work goes in and he never lives there. Picture painting every wall and never getting to hang your coat by the door.

explanations.answer: It will burn to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's a dramatic guess, friend. But Moses never says how it happens. He says, “You will build a house but will not live in it.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). The house isn't destroyed in the verse. He just never gets to live there.

explanations.answer: It will fall in a storm
explanations.explanation: I see where that came from. But Moses doesn't mention a storm. He says, “You will build a house but will not live in it.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). The verse doesn't say what happens to the house, only that he won't live in it.
Moses says the opposite, friend. He says, “You will plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). The man plants it and doesn't get the payoff. That's the sting of the curse.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “You will plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). The planting happens and the enjoying doesn't. It's the same kind of loss as the house right before it.

Yes, baker. Moses says their sons and daughters will be given to another nation, “…while your eyes grow weary looking for them day after day…” (Deuteronomy 28:32). I think this one hurts. Moses also says they will have no power in their hand.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “Your sons and daughters will be given to another nation, while your eyes grow weary looking for them day after day, with no power in your hand.” (Deuteronomy 28:32). I think this is one of the hardest lines in the whole list. The ones looking grow weary day after day, with no power in their hand.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “…there you will worship other gods—gods of wood and stone.” (Deuteronomy 28:36). Wood and stone! I've stamped plenty of dough in my day, and not one lump ever answered me back. That's the picture Moses paints, and it's a sad one: the LORD's people bowing to gods that can't hear a word.

Not quite, friend. In that nation Moses says they will worship “…other gods—gods of wood and stone.” (Deuteronomy 28:36). The sun and the moon aren't mentioned in that verse. Wood and stone are what he names.

explanations.answer: The LORD in a new temple
explanations.explanation: Hmm, Moses says something different, friend. In the nation they have never known, “…there you will worship other gods—gods of wood and stone.” (Deuteronomy 28:36). Other gods, not the LORD. A new temple isn't in that verse.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “You will sow much seed in the field but harvest little, because the locusts will consume it.” (Deuteronomy 28:38). Much seed goes in and little comes out. That's a lot of work for a very small payoff.

Not this time, friend. Moses says the harvest is little “…because the locusts will consume it.” (Deuteronomy 28:38). Much seed goes into the field and little comes out. The verse names locusts, not frogs.

Those are small, but the verse is after something bigger. Moses says the harvest is little “…because the locusts will consume it.” (Deuteronomy 28:38). Locusts are what he names here. Gnats aren't in this verse.

explanations.answer: He will rise higher and become the head
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says, “The foreigner living among you will rise higher and higher above you, while you sink down lower and lower.” (Deuteronomy 28:43). He adds, “He will be the head, and you will be the tail.” (Deuteronomy 28:44). The positions flip.

explanations.answer: He will leave the land for good
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Moses says the foreigner living among them “…will rise higher and higher above you…” (Deuteronomy 28:43). The verse has him going up while Israel sinks down lower and lower. Nothing in it says he leaves.

That's not what Moses says, friend. He says, “He will lend to you, but you will not lend to him. He will be the head, and you will be the tail.” (Deuteronomy 28:44). The verse is about lending and about who is head and who is tail. The word servant isn't in it.

explanations.answer: Serve the LORD with joy and gladness
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says, “Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance…” (Deuteronomy 28:47). He ties it to abundance. They had plenty and didn't serve with joy and gladness of heart.

explanations.answer: Share their riches with the poor
explanations.explanation: Good thought, but that isn't the reason Moses gives here. He says they “…did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance…” (Deuteronomy 28:47). The verse is about serving with joy and gladness. Sharing with the poor isn't named.

explanations.answer: Build a great temple for the LORD
explanations.explanation: I see why that's tempting, friend. But Moses says, “Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance…” (Deuteronomy 28:47). A temple isn't mentioned. He points to joy and gladness of heart.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “…you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution.” (Deuteronomy 28:48). He adds that the LORD will place an iron yoke on their neck. It's a heavy picture of a hard road.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, “…you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you…” (Deuteronomy 28:48). I get the guess, because neighbors sound a whole lot friendlier. But the ones they serve here are enemies, and Moses adds that an iron yoke goes on their neck. I think this is one of the hard lines in the chapter.

That's a different picture, friend. Moses says, “…you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution.” (Deuteronomy 28:48). Priests aren't part of this verse. The ones they serve are enemies.

Moses says the opposite, baker. The nation from afar is “…a nation whose language you will not understand…” (Deuteronomy 28:49). I'd be lost too if a stranger shouted orders at me in a language I'd never heard.

Yes, baker. Moses describes “…a nation whose language you will not understand…” (Deuteronomy 28:49). Picture it. Somebody is shouting at you, and you can't catch a single word. You'd just nod and smile like I do when a recipe is written in tiny letters. He says this nation comes from afar and swoops down like an eagle.

explanations.answer: No respect for the old and no pity for the young
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses calls it “…a ruthless nation with no respect for the old and no pity for the young.” (Deuteronomy 28:50). The old get no respect from it and the young get no pity. Ruthless is the word Moses picks.

explanations.answer: Respect for the old but no pity for the young
explanations.explanation: Half of that is right, friend. Moses says there will be “…no pity for the young.” But he also says “…no respect for the old…” (Deuteronomy 28:50). That's what makes the nation ruthless.

explanations.answer: Pity for the young but no respect for the old
explanations.explanation: Half of that matches, friend. Moses does say “…no respect for the old…” But he says “…no pity for the young.” too (Deuteronomy 28:50). It's both.

explanations.answer: The high fortified walls they trust in
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says they will besiege the cities “…until the high and fortified walls in which you trust have fallen.” (Deuteronomy 28:52). The walls are what they trust in, and they come down. It's a hard picture.

explanations.answer: The tents of their camp in the field
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Moses says the siege goes on “…until the high and fortified walls in which you trust have fallen.” (Deuteronomy 28:52). He's talking about city walls. Tents aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: The storehouses they built for grain
explanations.explanation: I can see why that came to mind, since the verse before says the nation will leave them no grain or new wine or oil (Deuteronomy 28:51). But the next verse says what falls is “…the high and fortified walls in which you trust…” (Deuteronomy 28:52). Storehouses aren't mentioned there.

Yes, baker. Moses says even “The most gentle and refined man among you…” will begrudge his brother, his wife and his surviving children (Deuteronomy 28:54). He has nothing left in the siege (Deuteronomy 28:55). I think this is one of the hardest parts of the whole passage.

It's true, friend, and it's hard to hear. Moses says “The most gentle and refined man among you…” will begrudge his brother, his wife and his surviving children (Deuteronomy 28:54). He has nothing left in the siege (Deuteronomy 28:55). I think this one hurts.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “He will afflict you again with all the diseases you dreaded in Egypt, and they will cling to you.” (Deuteronomy 28:60). The diseases they dreaded come back. That's one of the warnings he gives.

It's true, friend. Moses says, “He will afflict you again with all the diseases you dreaded in Egypt, and they will cling to you.” (Deuteronomy 28:60). The word again tells you they come back. Moses says it plainly.

Moses goes further than that, baker. He says the LORD will also bring “…every sickness and plague not recorded in this Book of the Law, until you are destroyed.” (Deuteronomy 28:61). So it doesn't stop at the ones written down.

Yes, baker. Moses says the LORD will also bring “…every sickness and plague not recorded in this Book of the Law, until you are destroyed.” (Deuteronomy 28:61). The list in the book isn't the end of it. That's a sobering line.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 28:62). From stars to few. That's quite a drop.
That's the opposite, friend. Moses says, “You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number…” (Deuteronomy 28:62). They go from many to few. The word is few.
Good guess, but the verse is about numbers. Moses says, “You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number…” (Deuteronomy 28:62). Few is the word. Strong isn't in it.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other…” (Deuteronomy 28:64). That comes after he says they will be uprooted from the land they are entering to possess (Deuteronomy 28:63). He adds that there they will worship other gods, gods of wood and stone.

Not quite, friend. Moses says the LORD will scatter them “…among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other…” (Deuteronomy 28:64). That's far bigger than one wilderness. It's all the nations.

Close to home, but Moses says something much wider. The LORD will scatter them “…among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other…” (Deuteronomy 28:64). Gilead isn't named. He means every nation.

Yes, baker. Moses says they will say those words “…because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see.” (Deuteronomy 28:67). I think that means no hour feels safe to them. That's a hard way to live.
Not this one, friend. Moses says the words come “…because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see.” (Deuteronomy 28:67). The word is dread. Pride isn't in it.

Not quite, friend. Moses says the words come “…because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see.” (Deuteronomy 28:67). It's dread that fills their hearts. Greed isn't in the verse.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “There you will sell yourselves to your enemies as male and female slaves, but no one will buy you.” (Deuteronomy 28:68). They offer themselves and nobody takes the offer. I think that's about as low as it gets, and it closes out Moses' list of curses.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will buy them all
explanations.explanation: Not what Moses says, friend. He says they will sell themselves as slaves, “…but no one will buy you.” (Deuteronomy 28:68). Nobody buys them at all. It's a bleak ending.

Hmm, there's no Pharaoh in that verse, friend. Moses says they will sell themselves to their enemies as slaves, “…but no one will buy you.” (Deuteronomy 28:68). The verse ends with no buyer. Being set free isn't in it, and it's the last picture in Moses' list of curses.
